summary: Intermittent assume-role failures due to mismatched session tag attribute encoding between GCP WIF and AWS STS
description: Summary: Jobs that bootstrap dedicated GPU provisioners via the auth-proxy intermittently fail to assume the target AWS role. Errors show AccessDenied: Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRole or downstream permission checks fail when role session tags parsed by the provisioner are missing expected attributes. This started after last week's auth-proxy update that changed WIF-to-STS attribute normalization. Impact: Several Dedicated onboarding runs and internal automated repro jobs failed, blocking a small number of customer onboarding tasks and delaying a production scale test. Intermittent: ~10% of assume-role attempts in the last 48h failed.
impact: Dedicated provisioning jobs intermittently fail to assume AWS roles; blocks internal repros and delays a handful of customer onboards. Estimated affected jobs: ~12/day during peak.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Trigger the dedicated onboarding pipeline that uses GCP WIF->AWS role federation through auth-proxy
2) Observe the auth-proxy logs for request->response attribute mapping
3) In failing cases, the provisioner logs show downstream permission errors referencing missing 'env' or truncated 'role-session' attributes
4) Re-run with verbose STS debug: CloudTrail shows AssumeRole succeeded but session tags truncated/rewritten; provisioner denies due to absent tag guardrails
investigation_notes: Auth-proxy change on 2026-03-08 started normalizing multivalue attributes into a single JSON-encoded string; this appears to exceed AWS STS tag length in some flows
CloudTrail evidence: 90% of failed AssumeRole calls return 200 with AssumedRoleUser but the session tag list is shorter than expected (missing 'env' or 'team')

GCP audit logs: WIF token contained attributes 'environment=prod' and 'team=platform', auth-proxy forwarded 'attributes' as 'attrs:{"environment":"prod","team":"platform"}' string which STS interprets as a single tag 'attrs' instead of separate tags
Provisioner enforces tag-based RBAC: expects 'env' and 'team' top-level tags; when tags are absent permission engine rejects requests
Reproduced locally by issuing WIF with long attribute payload -> AWS STS drops tags beyond 64 characters per tag key/value limit

Hypothesis: two contributing factors — auth-proxy JSON-encoding of attributes and STS per-tag length/truncation behavior. Some attribute values combined in a single tag causing guardrail checks to fail.
workarounds_tried: 1) Temporary rollback of auth-proxy normalization to previous behavior — confirmed immediate reduction in failures in a small canary cluster
2) Short-term change in provisioner RBAC to accept 'attrs' combined tag (risk: weakens policy precision) — tested in staging, allowed repro jobs to proceed
3) Manual re-run of blocked onboards after rolling back auth-proxy in controlled window
proposed_fix: Primary fix: update auth-proxy attribute mapping to emit individual STS session tags per attribute (key->value) and ensure each tag respects AWS limits (max 128 characters for value, 128 for key). Add explicit truncation/validation and a feature-flag to opt-in. Secondary: harden provisioner to parse combined 'attrs' tag as JSON only after verifying tag presence, emit a telemetry metric when fallback parsing is used.
risk_and_rollout_notes: Change must be rolled out to auth-proxy instances in all regions. Rollout steps: (1) add validation and flag disabled by default; (2) enable in canary in eu-west-1 for 24h; (3) monitor CloudTrail and provisioner RBAC metrics; (4) progressively enable across us-east-1 and other regions. Provisioner RBAC fallback should be maintained until full rollforward confirmed. Backout: revert to previous auth-proxy image.
resolution: In progress — a patch branch has been opened that splits attributes into individual tags and enforces per-tag length limits. Canaries scheduled for eu-west-1 on 2026-03-12. Full rollout pending successful 24h canary. Temporary mitigation (auth-proxy rollback) reduced failures; provisioner fallback parsing remains as secondary safety net.
